title: Harness Handbook: Making Evolving Agent Harnesses Readable,Navigable, and Editable
event_hint: Harness Handbook + BGPD: a behavior-centric handbook for agent harnesses improves behavior localization and edit-plan quality with fewer planner tokens.
problem: Behavior localization is a central bottleneck in evolving production agent harnesses: a modification request describes what behavior should change, but the repository is organized by files/functions/modules, while a single behavior is distributed across many nonadjacent sites spanning execution stages and shared state. Existing code search, repository maps, summarization, and long-context editing make code easier to inspect but still leave developers/agents to recover the behavior-to-code mapping by hand, and agents with limited context may overlook scattered or rarely executed paths.
mechanism: Harness Handbook is a behavior-centric representation built automatically in three phases: Phase I deterministic static fact extraction (language adapters parse functions, boundaries, signatures, call edges; unresolved calls are logged, not guessed; no LLM calls); Phase II behavioral organization maps source units onto an execution-stage skeleton using either function-as-leaf (when a reliable seed skeleton exists and function-level entries fit budget) or file-as-leaf (repository scale) modes; Phase III hierarchical synthesis produces an L1-L3 document tree plus cross-stage state registers, with each entry linked to a statically identified source location. Behavior-Guided Progressive Disclosure (BGPD) guides agents from high-level behaviors down to implementation details and verifies candidate locations against current source; an automatic resynchronization step updates the handbook on repository change, limiting model calls to four semantic steps (classification, file assignment, within-stage organization, description revision).

evidence.claim: Handbook-Assisted planning raises overall win rates vs Baseline by 10.0 percentage points on Codex and 18.9 points on Terminus-2.
evidence.condition: 30 modification requests per harness; two harnesses (Codex Rust file-as-leaf, Terminus-2 Python function-as-leaf); Handbook-Assisted BGPD vs Baseline arms

evidence.claim: Planner token use falls by 12.7% on Codex and 8.6% on Terminus-2 with handbook assistance.
evidence.condition: Same planning tasks on the two evaluated harnesses

evidence.claim: With handbook guidance a weaker planner matches stronger reference models on Terminus-2: file-level F1 84.7% and 89.3%, symbol-level F1 77.1% and 89.3% against Opus 4.8 and GPT-5.5 references; precision reaches 93.3% against GPT-5.5 at both granularities.
evidence.value: File F1 84.7/89.3, symbol F1 77.1/89.3; precision 93.3% vs GPT-5.5
evidence.condition: Terminus-2; weaker planner + handbook; all 24 file/symbol Recall/Precision/F1 comparisons improved against two independent references
evidence.source_locator: Section 4.2 and Section 5 Conclusion, PDF Page 10

evidence.claim: Complete localization failures (Wrong = zero overlap vs reference) never increase with the handbook and fall by as much as 25.9 points.
evidence.value: up to 25.9 points reduction in Wrong rate

evidence.claim: All six harness-by-type win-rate comparisons favor the Handbook-Assisted arm, with gains of 16.3 to 33.3 percentage points; cross-file requests improve 16.3 and 20.0 points; Codex gains most on Query requests (+26.7) and Terminus-2 most on Search-Hostile requests (+33.3).
evidence.condition: Stratified by request type and localization difficulty across the two harnesses

evaluation_context: Two open-source agent harnesses differing by roughly two orders of magnitude: Terminus-2 (Python terminal agent from the Harbor framework, observe-decide-act loop over tmux; 6 source files, 103 internal-function nodes, 41 boundary nodes, 257 resolved call edges; function-as-leaf; built handbook has 20 L2 stages, 106 L3 entries, 10 state registers) and Codex (Rust monorepo behind the Codex coding agent; 2,267 files, 34,363 internal-function nodes, 4,016 boundary nodes, 159,960 resolved call edges; file-as-leaf; 140 L2 stages, 2,267 L3 entries, 62 state registers). 30 modification requests per harness balanced across request type and localization difficulty; two arms (Baseline vs Handbook-Assisted BGPD) with every factor other than handbook access held fixed; reference localization plans from Opus 4.8 and GPT-5.5.
limitations: Validated on only two harnesses (though they differ sharply in scale and language). Static analysis is conservative: unresolved calls are logged rather than assigned guessed targets, and content that cannot be parsed/classified is frozen or recorded in the coverage record. The specific weaker planner model whose F1/precision are reported is not named in the visible front evidence. Gain variation is not fully explained by labeled difficulty. The paper reports planning/localization quality and planner-token cost, not end-to-end executed task success rate or wall-clock latency, and the initial handbook construction cost is only partially specified (resynchronization is limited to four model steps).
project_relevance: Directly addresses the Agent语义加速 question of cutting repeated Read/Grep/context localization: a behavior-centric index lets an agent navigate from a requested behavior to source sites instead of iteratively exploring files, and it reports exactly the metrics the topic values (planner-token reduction of 12.7%/8.6% and localization F1/Precision). Caveat for project inference: it measures edit-plan/localization quality, not end-to-end task latency or success rate, and build/resync cost is only partly quantified; net benefit and applicability to general (non-harness) code search still need confirmation from later sections.

evidence_gaps.question: Which specific planner model is the weaker planner whose F1/precision are reported against the Opus 4.8 and GPT-5.5 references, and is it the same across both harnesses?
What is the initial Handbook construction cost (Phase I-III) in tokens/model calls/time, and does the paper report a net cost-benefit including build plus resynchronization?
Does the paper report any downstream end-to-end task success rate or wall-clock latency from executing the Handbook-Assisted plans, beyond plan-quality and planner-token metrics?
